text:
For Alfred Okugbeni, Managing Director of Nigerian Sinotruck Limited, the road from banking halls to the heart of the nation’s haulage industry has been anything but straightforward. But through grit, reinvention and a pragmatic vision, Okugbeni has set about building more than a truck business, writes Adedayo Adejobi
From navigating banking halls to being Nigeria’s haulage backbone, Alfred Okugbeni’s journey is a masterclass on setbacks, reinvention, and industrial grit.
Fourteen years ago, Nigerian Sinotruck Limited entered Nigeria’s haulage industry with quiet ambition. Few would have predicted the scale and significance of its eventual footprint. Today, it stands as a compelling symbol of tenacity, innovation, and a deep-rooted commitment to reshaping the nation’s logistics landscape through rugged, adaptive and locally responsive transport solutions.
As the Managing Director, Okugbeni’s story is not one of linear progression, but of disappointment, recalibration, and persistent rebuilding in one of the world’s most unforgiving business environments.
In his modest Surulere office, layered with files, vehicle-part catalogues, and Sinotruk prototypes, Okugbeni speaks with measured conviction. His cadence is calm, but his narrative carries weight shaped by experience rather than rhetoric.
“This is one of the most challenging business environments on the planet,” he reflects. “Infrastructure is weak, policies change overnight, and multiple regulatory bodies often see private business as a source of rent, not a partner in progress.”
Long before he ventured into the haulage business, Okugbeni was a young professional, developing habits that would later inform his worldview. During his National Youth Service year in 1997 at Dunlop PLC, and in the early years of his banking career at UBA, he cultivated what he describes as a discipline of “reading for direction.”
Among the publications that shaped his intellectual curiosity was THISDAY newspaper—not as a defining force, but as part of a broader habit of engaging with ideas on leadership, business and global thinking.
He recalls encountering a feature summarising Stephen Covey’s The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People in THISDAY at a formative stage of his career.
“The values Covey espoused mirrored principles I already held dear,” he reflects. “Discipline, proactivity, and prioritising the important over the urgent—it all resonated.”
When the newspaper later serialised Covey’s work during his early banking years, he followed it with interest, collecting editions where possible.
“That commitment to thought leadership and the balanced editorial stance stood out,” he says.
“Over time, I also appreciated the boldness of its editorial voice and its Chairman, Nduka Obaigbena.”
For Okugbeni, such engagements were part of a wider intellectual diet that helped shape his thinking, but not the sole architect of it. They reinforced an already forming orientation towards discipline, systems thinking, and long-term structure.
Okugbeni and his team ran a logistics venture built around European trucks. On paper, the model appeared robust. In practice, it collided with Nigeria’s operational realities.
“We were servicing loans on expensive trucks, dealing with untrained drivers, and managing spare parts we couldn’t locally source,” he recalls.
The business eventually collapsed under financial strain. But failure, in his telling, was not an endpoint; it was a correction.
Out of that experience emerged a sharper understanding of Nigeria’s transport ecosystem and a conviction that success required adaptation rather than importation of foreign templates. That realisation led him to Sinotruk, a Chinese manufacturer known for rugged, affordable and mechanically adaptable trucks suited to harsh operating conditions.
By 2012, Nigerian Sinotruck Limited was formally incorporated. By 2019, it secured a distribution agreement with Sinotruk in China. What began as a modest import and sales operation gradually evolved into a full logistics solutions company.
Today, its 4S model—Showroom, Spare Parts, Survey, Sales and Servicing—defines its operational identity and distinguishes it within a highly competitive sector.
“We don’t just sell trucks,” Okugbeni explains. “We offer uptime.”
That philosophy has become central to its value proposition, particularly for fleet operators and multinational companies managing large-scale logistics across difficult terrain.
Beyond sales, the company has invested heavily in after-sales support, technical training, and rapid-response maintenance systems.
From roadside recovery teams to structured fleet servicing for hundreds of vehicles, Nigerian Sinotruck Limited has positioned itself not just as a supplier, but as an operational partner.
Despite its progress, Okugbeni remains candid about structural constraints in Nigeria’s industrial environment.
“When the government launched the National Automotive Industry Development Plan in 2012, it gave us hope. We invested in SKD assembly,” he says. “But over time, implementation weakened.”
“Today, fully built vehicles are easier and cheaper to import. So why assemble? We’re not just importing trucks—we’re exporting jobs.”
For him, this reflects a broader disconnect between industrial policy ambition and execution.
“Nigeria has the raw materials, the market, and the manpower,” he insists. “What we lack is coordination and political will.”
Despite these challenges, Nigerian Sinotruck Limited continues to invest in localisation through assembly capacity and a growing technical training academy, which Okugbeni envisions evolving into a full institute for mechanical and logistics engineering.
“We are actively building what I hope will become one of the premier technical institutes in West Africa,” he says.
At its core is a philosophy that extends beyond corporate expansion: skills development as national infrastructure.
“We’re not just talking about youth empowerment. We’re investing in it,” he adds. “We want to bring dignity back to technical work and formalise an ecosystem that has existed informally for decades.”
He is equally concerned about shifting youth aspirations in a difficult economic environment.
“It’s not sustainable,” he says of shortcuts to wealth. “We need to show young Nigerians that technical careers can be fulfilling, respectable, and prosperous.”
Even within operational constraints, the company is positioning itself for future transitions. It has been active in compressed natural gas (CNG) truck deployment for over three years and is exploring electric mobility solutions.
“We see gas as a transitional fuel while Nigeria builds capacity in renewables,” he explains. “Eventually, we will move into hydrogen and fully electric fleets.”
He is quick to clarify misconceptions around safety concerns.
“CNG is safe when used correctly. The issues we’ve seen stem from unprofessional retrofitting, often using inappropriate materials and methods.”
The company has introduced Sitrak electric trucks to help businesses reduce haulage costs, improve distribution efficiency and strengthen industrial competitiveness. We are initially targeting intra-city deliveries; the trucks offer a reported daily range of up to 200 kilometres, lower maintenance requirements and potential operating cost savings of 40–50 per cent, depending on operating conditions. The unique appeal lies in combining energy efficiency with practical fleet operations, particularly for manufacturers with overnight charging capacity.
“One of the major ways to crack this is to bring in low-cost operating vehicles. And the electric truck fits very well into that.” Beyond cost savings, the initiative could support local vehicle assembly, skills development and Nigeria’s broader industrial growth.
In an industry often shaped by short-term survival tactics, Okugbeni insists on a different foundation. “We don’t chase government contracts. We don’t offer bribes. We focus on delivering value. In Nigeria, integrity is a competitive advantage, even if the rewards are not immediate.”
It is a principle that has defined both resilience and reputation.
As Nigeria embarks on ambitious infrastructure development—from highways to rail expansion—the demand for efficient haulage systems is expected to rise sharply. Okugbeni believes his company is positioned within that trajectory.
“We’re not just selling machines,” he says. “We’re part of the national development puzzle.”
